title: Unlimited is a reserved sentinel value that short-circuits all rate-limit accounting rather than a very large number
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.3 sets an unlimited limit as `setRateLimitData(key, type(uint256).max, 0, type(uint256).max, block.timestamp)`, and both trigger functions special-case it: `if (maxAmount == type(uint256).max) return type(uint256).max;` (A...1.3.4, A...1.3.5). The query function does the same before any arithmetic (A...1.3.1).

The short-circuit is doing three jobs. It avoids the overflow that `slope * elapsed + lastAmount` would otherwise risk near the type maximum. It avoids a storage write on every operation through an unlimited key, which is the common case for outflows and is the dominant gas cost. And it makes "unlimited" a distinguishable state rather than a threshold nobody expects to cross.

The trade-off is observability. Because the decrease returns before touching `lastAmount`, an unlimited key accumulates **no record** of how much has flowed through it. Given that every documented instance sets its outflow to unlimited, the on-chain rate-limit state offers no view of outflow volume at all; monitoring that has to come from events emitted by the controller functions instead.

Note also the deliberate slope of `0` in the unlimited configuration — with the sentinel maxAmount the slope is unreachable, so it is set to zero to signal that replenishment is meaningless here rather than merely fast.
description: maxAmount == type(uint256).max makes both trigger functions return early without writing state, so unlimited keys are cheap and overflow-proof but leave no usage trail.
